## Lecture overview

<br>

- Why do sample means tend to follow a normal distribution?
- How can we use a sample to estimate a population mean?
- What is a confidence interval?
- When should we use the normal distribution or the $t$-distribution?
- Can we estimate uncertainty without relying on theoretical distributions?

## The Central Limit Theorem {style="font-size: 75%;"}

### Why do sample means matter?

Suppose we want to understand the average value of a variable in a population.

For example:

- The average height of adults in Ireland.
- The average examination score of university students.
- The average weight of products manufactured by a company.

Usually, we cannot measure the entire population. So we collect a sample
and calculate its mean:

$$
\bar{X}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i
$$

::: {.callout-warning}
## But how much would this sample mean change if we collected a different sample?

This is where the [Central Limit Theorem]{.alert} becomes useful.
:::

## The Central Limit Theorem

<br>

::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
Under appropriate conditions, the distribution of sample means becomes
approximately normal as the sample size increases.
:::

Imagine repeatedly:

- Taking a random sample from a population.
- Calculating the sample mean.
- Repeating this process many times.

::: {.callout-tip}
## The resulting collection of sample means forms a sampling distribution.

For sufficiently large sample sizes, this distribution will be approximately
normal, even if the original population is not normally distributed.
:::

## The Central Limit Theorem

### Let's take an example

Consider rolling a fair six-sided die.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

The possible outcomes are

$$
X\in{1,2,3,4,5,6}
$$

:::
::: {.column}

Each outcome is equally likely

$$
P(X = x) = \frac{1}{6}
$$

:::
::::

[The population distribution is therefore uniform]{.center}

## The Central Limit Theorem

### Let's take an example

<br>

```{r}
#| label: chunk-1

die_data <- tibble(face = 1:6, probability = rep(1 / 6, 6))

die_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = face, y = probability)) +
  geom_col(fill = blue_col, colour = "black", width = 0.7) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:6) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of a fair die roll",
    x = "Die face",
    y = "Probability"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## The sampling distribution of the mean

Now let's repeat the process 1,000 times.

Each time:

- Roll a die 100 times.
- Calculate the sample mean.
- Store that mean.

We can then examine the distribution of the 1,000 sample means.

---

<br>

```{r}
#| label: chunk-3

n_samples <- 1000
sample_size <- 100

sample_means <- replicate(
  n_samples,
  mean(sample(1:6, size = sample_size, replace = TRUE))
)

hist(
  sample_means,
  breaks = 25,
  col = blue_col,
  main = "Sampling distribution of the mean",
  xlab = "Sample mean"
)
```

---

<br>

```{r}
#| label: chunk-sup-1
p <- dice_means |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(id = row_number()) |>
  tidyr::crossing(frame = seq(1, 1000, by = 10)) |>
  filter(id <= frame) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25, fill = blue_col, colour = "black") +
  labs(title = "Sampling distribution", x = "Sample mean", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  gganimate::transition_states(
    states = frame,
    transition_length = 2,
    state_length = 1
  ) +
  gganimate::ease_aes("cubic-in-out")

gganimate::animate(p, nframes = 200, fps = 20)
```


---

<br>

```{r}
#| label: chunk-4

p1 <- ggplot(tibble(x = 1:6), aes(x)) +
  geom_bar(fill = blue_col, colour = "black", width = 0.7) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:6) +
  labs(title = "Population distribution", x = "Die roll", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

p2 <- ggplot(tibble(x = dice_one), aes(x)) +
  geom_bar(fill = blue_col, colour = "black", width = 0.7) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:6) +
  labs(title = "One sample", x = "Die roll", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

p3 <- ggplot(tibble(x = dice_means), aes(x)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25, fill = blue_col, colour = "black") +
  labs(title = "Sampling distribution", x = "Sample mean", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

patchwork::wrap_plots(p1, p2, p3)
```

:::{.notes}
The population and individual sample distributions are discrete, while the
sampling distribution of the means is approximately bell-shaped.
:::

## The Central Limit Theorem {style="font-size: 60%;"}

### Mathematically

If we take independent observations from a population with:

- Mean $\mu$
- Standard deviation $\sigma$

Then, for a sufficiently large sample size $n$, the sampling distribution of
the sample mean is approximately:

$$
\bar{X}\approx N\left(\mu,\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)
$$

Equivalently, its standard error is:

$$
SE(\bar{X})=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
$$

::: {.callout-important}
## The important properties are:

- The mean of the sample means is $\mu$.
- The standard error of the sample means is $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$.
- The distribution becomes approximately normal as $n$ increases, under the CLT conditions.
:::

## What happens as sample size increases? {style="font-size: 70%;"}

The standard error is:

$$
SE(\bar{X})=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
$$

[**As the sample size increases, the standard error decreases.**]{.center}

```{r}
#| label: chunk-5

sample_sizes <- c(10, 25, 50, 100, 250)

se_data <- tibble(
  n = sample_sizes,
  standard_error = sqrt(35 / 12) / sqrt(sample_sizes)
)

se_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = standard_error)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = blue_col) +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Effect of sample size on standard error",
    x = "Sample size",
    y = "Standard error"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Standard errors and confidence intervals {style="font-size: 75%;"}

### Estimating the standard error

In practice, we usually do not know the population standard deviation $\sigma$.

Instead, we estimate it using the sample standard deviation $s$.

$$
SE(\bar{X})=\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
$$

where:

- $s$ is the sample standard deviation.
- $n$ is the sample size.

The standard error tells us how much we would expect the sample mean to
vary across repeated samples.

::: {.callout-important}
## Remember the difference

- **Standard deviation**: variability of individual observations.
- **Standard error**: variability of sample means.

:::

## From the sampling distribution to a confidence interval {style="font-size: 75%;"}

Suppose the sampling distribution of the sample mean is approximately normal.

Approximately 95% of the area under the standard normal curve lies
between -1.96 and 1.96.

$$
P(-1.96 < Z < 1.96) \approx 0.95
$$

Using the standard error:

$$
P\left(-1.96<\frac{\bar{X}-\mu}{SE(\bar{X})} <1.96 \right)\approx0.95
$$


::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Rearranging gives:

$$
P\left(\bar{X}-1.96SE(\bar{X}) < \mu < \bar{X}+1.96SE(\bar{X}) \right) \approx 0.95
$$

This gives us the familiar 95% confidence interval:

$$
\boxed{
\bar{X}\pm1.96\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
}
$$

:::

## Interpreting a 95% confidence interval {style="font-size: 90%;"}

Suppose we calculate a 95% confidence interval for the average examination score
where the lower bound is $62$ and the upper bound is $68$

<br>

::: {.callout-note}
## We are 95% confident that the population mean examination score lies between 62 and 68."
:::

<br>

::: {.callout-tip}
## What does 95% confidence actually mean?

If we repeatedly collected samples and calculated a 95% confidence interval
each time, approximately 95% of those intervals would contain the true
population mean.
:::

## What if the sample size is small? {style="font-size: 80%;"}

The normal approximation is **useful for large samples**, but what happens
when we have a **small sample**?

- Suppose we take a random sample from a population that is approximately
  normally distributed.
- We want to estimate the population mean,
  but we do not know the population standard deviation.


::: {.callout-tip}
## In this situation, we use the Student's $t$-distribution.

The test statistic is:

$$
T=\frac{\bar{X}-\mu}{s/\sqrt{n}}
$$

Under the assumption of an independent random sample from a normal population:

$$
T\sim t_{n-1}
$$

The (t)-distribution accounts for the additional uncertainty from
estimating the population standard deviation using the sample
:::


## Comparing the normal and t-distributions

<br>

```{r}
#| label: chunk-6

x <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 500)

comparison <- tibble(
  x = x,
  normal = dnorm(x),
  t = dt(x, df = 5)
) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = c(normal, t),
    names_to = "distribution",
    values_to = "density"
  )

ggplot(comparison, aes(x, density, colour = distribution)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  ggokabeito::scale_colour_okabe_ito() +
  labs(
    title = "Normal distribution versus t-distribution",
    x = "Value",
    y = "Density",
    colour = "Distribution"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Confidence intervals using the t-distribution {style="font-size: 70%;"}

::: {.panel-tabset}

## In theory

For a sample from an approximately normal population with unknown standard deviation, the 95% confidence interval for the population mean is:

$$
\boxed{
\bar{X}\pm t_{n-1,0.975}\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
}
$$

where:

- $\bar{X}$ is the sample mean.
- $s$ is the sample standard deviation.
- $n$ is the sample size.
- $t_{n-1,0.975}$ is the 97.5th percentile of the $t$-distribution with $n-1$
  degrees of freedom.

## In practice

Suppose we have:


:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="33%"}

$$\bar{X} = 20$$

:::

::: {.column width="33%"}

$$s = 4$$

:::

::: {.column width="33%"}

$$n = 10$$

:::
::::


::: {.fragment .fade-up}
First, calculate the standard error:

$$
SE=\frac{4}{\sqrt{10}}
$$

:::


::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Then calculate the critical value:

```{r}
#| label: chunk-7
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true

critical_value <- qt(0.975, df = 9)
critical_value
```

$$20 \pm 2.262157 \times 4/\sqrt{10} = (17.14, 22.86)$$
:::

## Code

```{r}
#| label: chunk-7b
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true

critical_value <- qt(0.975, df = 9)
critical_value
```

```{r}
#| label: chunk-8b
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true

sample_mean <- 20
sample_sd <- 4
n <- 10

se <- sample_sd / sqrt(n)

lower <- sample_mean - critical_value * se
upper <- sample_mean + critical_value * se

round(c(lower, upper), digits = 2)
```

:::

## Bootstrapping {style="font-size: 80%;"}

So far, we have relied on theoretical probability distributions to
estimate uncertainty.

But what if:

- The sample is very small?
- The population distribution is unknown?
- We are unsure whether a theoretical distribution is appropriate?

**One alternative is bootstrapping**

::: {.callout-warning appearance="minimal"}
Bootstrapping is a resampling method that uses the observed sample to
estimate the sampling distribution of a statistic.

Instead of repeatedly sampling from the original population, we repeatedly
sample from the data we have collected.
:::

## Bootstrapping {style="font-size: 80%;"}

### How does it work

Suppose we collect a sample of five used cars and record their selling prices.

We want to estimate the average selling price in the wider population.

$$
X \in \{18300, \; 20100, \; 9600, \; 10700, \; 27000\}
$$

::: {.callout-note}
## How to bootstrap

1. Start with the original sample.
2. Randomly select observations from that sample, with replacement.
3. Keep the bootstrap sample the same size as the original sample.
4. Calculate the statistic of interest, such as the mean.
5. Repeat many times

[**The resulting statistics form a bootstrap distribution**]{.center}

:::

---

<br>


::: {.panel-tabset}

## Figure

```{r}
#| label: chunk-9a

# The data
car_data <- c(18300, 20100, 9600, 10700, 27000)

# Number of bootstrap samples
n_boot <- 1000

# Do bootsrapping
bootstrap_means <- replicate(
  n_boot,
  mean(sample(car_data, replace = TRUE))
)

# Plot
hist(
  bootstrap_means,
  breaks = 25,
  col = "steelblue",
  main = "Bootstrap distribution of the mean",
  xlab = "Bootstrap sample mean"
)
```

## Code

```{r}
#| label: chunk-9
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# The data
car_data <- c(18300, 20100, 9600, 10700, 27000)

# Number of bootstrap samples
n_boot <- 1000

# Do bootsrapping
bootstrap_means <- replicate(
  n_boot,
  mean(sample(car_data, replace = TRUE))
)

# Plot
hist(
  bootstrap_means,
  breaks = 25,
  col = "steelblue",
  main = "Bootstrap distribution of the mean",
  xlab = "Bootstrap sample mean"
)
```

:::

## Bootstrap percentile confidence intervals

A percentile confidence interval uses the quantiles of the
bootstrap distribution.

```{r}
#| label: chunk-10
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true

quantile(bootstrap_means, probs = c(0.025, 0.975))
```

---

<br>
<br>

::: {.callout-important}

## Bootstrapping is useful, but it is not a solution to every problem

Bootstrap samples are generated from the original observed data.

The method assumes the [original sample provides a reasonable
representation of the population]{.alert}.

- Very small samples may not capture the full variability of the population.
- Unusual observations can have a substantial influence on bootstrap estimates.
- In our used-car example, we only have five observations.
- The bootstrap distribution is therefore based on a very limited representation of the population.
- A larger, more representative original sample would generally provide a more reliable basis for bootstrapping.

:::
